passage: By October Damini had twelve small students on the veranda in three batches, from four in the afternoon till nine at night. The first fee money had made her giddy, and every new child felt like another win. The steel tin behind the rice sack grew heavy. But her own homework was done on the bus, half-copied, and she slept five hours. In the monthly test her maths marks fell from sixty-eight to forty-one. “Your notebook's empty,” her friend Ira said at lunch. Damini snapped that she was earning. That night she sat with the marked test in one hand and the tin in the other, counting both. The rupees suddenly looked small beside everything they had cost.

qa.q: How many students did Damini have by October?
What was Damini feeling when Ira said the notebook was empty?
qa.a: Defensive and stung: she snapped that she was earning, though the falling marks were already worrying her.

qa.q: What could Damini do instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: She could keep only a few students on fixed evenings and protect sleep and homework time, because steady marks and rest matter more than extra money.

qa.q: How might Ira see Damini's plan?
qa.a: Ira sees a friend who is tired, short-tempered and behind on homework, and worries that the tutoring is costing more than it earns.

grounding: Excited by early earnings, a student takes on many tutees, and homework, sleep and marks suffer.

passage:
In Accra, Ada started tutoring one boy in maths after school and earned more in a week than she'd ever had. Her friend Abebe was impressed. "Take more!"

She did. By the end of the month she had seven students: Monday to Saturday, some evenings two in a row. Her own homework shifted to after ten. Sleep came at one, sometimes later.

Her chemistry teacher returned a test marked 11 out of 30. Ada stared at it. She'd scored 25 on the last one.

At lunch, Abebe asked, "You okay? You look awful."

"I'm fine. I'm earning."

But that night, looking at her notes for the three tutoring lessons she hadn't prepared, and her own chemistry homework untouched, she did the maths. The money was good. But she was trading her own grades and sleep for it, and that trade didn't look good at all.

qa.q: How many students did Ada have by the end of the month?
How did Ada feel seeing the 11 out of 30?
qa.a: She felt shocked and uneasy, having scored 25 on the last test.

qa.q: What would you change first in Ada's tutoring plan?
qa.a: Cut back to a small, fixed number of students and protect time for her own homework and sleep, maybe with her parents' input.

qa.q: How does Abebe see Ada's situation?
qa.a: Abebe first encouraged more students but now seems worried, noticing she looks awful.

grounding: Shows a student excited by early earnings taking on many tutoring students until homework and sleep suffer, marks fall and the money looks like a poor trade.

passage:
The tuition centre on the second floor of the shopping complex was noisy with coolers. Mridul had been tutoring there for three months, Class 6 maths, after his own coaching. At first two students. Now nine, in three batches, five evenings a week.

The centre manager, Hemant Sir, came by during the break. "Your results?"

Mridul showed his phone: his physics unit test, 14 out of 40. His last one had been 32.

"You're good with the kids," Hemant Sir said. "But you're in Class 12. What's the board exam worth to you, compared to this?"

Mridul didn't answer. He'd been sleeping at one. He'd skipped two coaching tests to cover a batch. The money was going into a savings box he hadn't even opened.

"I'm always tired," he admitted. "I thought the money made it worth it."

"Does it?" Hemant Sir asked.

qa.q: How many students was Mridul tutoring now?
qa.a: Nine, in three batches, five evenings a week.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when he admitted he was always tired?
qa.a: He felt worn out and uneasy, starting to doubt that the money made it worth it.

qa.q: What else could Mridul do before his board exam?
qa.a: He could talk to his parents and Hemant Sir about reducing to one batch or pausing until after boards, so study and sleep come first.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Hemant Sir?
qa.a: Hemant Sir values Mridul's teaching but seems concerned, seeing the falling marks as too high a price.

grounding: Shows a student who took on many tutoring batches after early earnings, with sleep, study and marks suffering until the money looks like a poor trade.
